## 1.1 Background and Context

(target: 600 words)

The European Union's health sector is undergoing the most significant data-governance transformation in its history. In March 2025, the European Health Data Space Regulation (EU) 2025/327 entered into force, establishing the first Union-wide legal framework for the primary and secondary use of electronic health data across all Member States and European Economic Area countries (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2025). The regulation creates a binding architecture for cross-border exchange of patient summaries, electronic prescriptions, laboratory results, medical imaging, and hospital discharge reports, with primary-use exchange of patient summaries and ePrescriptions becoming mandatory across the EU and EEA by March 2029, and the remaining priority categories by March 2031 (European Commission, 2025a).

The technical infrastructure underpinning this regulatory shift is MyHealth@EU, the federated pull-based system that allows a clinician in one Member State to retrieve a patient summary or dispense an ePrescription issued in another Member State. Each participating country operates a single National Contact Point for eHealth (NCPeH), and all cross-border exchanges flow through a six-step gateway protocol implemented in the Open National Contact Point (OpenNCP) software stack. These six steps cover service discovery, patient discovery, document retrieval, pivot translation between national clinical document formats and a common European format, security and consent validation, and audit logging (Simjanoska Misheva et al., 2025).

Norway is in the late stages of operational integration with MyHealth@EU. The Norwegian connection project began in January 2023 under joint coordination between the Norwegian Directorate of Health (Helsedirektoratet) and the Norwegian Health Network (Norsk Helsenett SF), with go-live piloting scheduled for 2025 alongside Austria, Cyprus, Denmark, Hungary, Iceland, Italy, Romania, Slovenia, and Sweden (European Commission, 2025b). As Norway is not a Member State of the European Union but an EEA member, EHDS implementation is being processed through the EEA Joint Committee, with the Norwegian Directorate of Health having delivered its formal EHDS gap analysis on 11 April 2025 (Helsedirektoratet, 2025a).

Within this regulatory transformation, the most consequential change for clinical practice is the new layer of patient rights established by EHDS. Citizens gain the right to access and download their electronic health data, to view full logs of who has accessed it, to set granular restrictions on cross-border sharing, and to opt out of secondary use (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2025). These rights interact directly with two long-standing technical standards. The first is IHE Audit Trail and Node Authentication (ATNA), the integration profile that defines how access events are logged in cross-border exchanges. Under the eHDSI specification adopted for MyHealth@EU, ATNA-compliant audit repositories must retain logs for a minimum of ten years (Simjanoska Misheva et al., 2025). The second is the General Data Protection Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2016/679), whose Article 17 establishes the data subject's right to obtain erasure of personal data without undue delay under specified conditions (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2016).

A third constraint is now emerging from the implementing infrastructure for EHDS secondary use. The draft Guideline for Health Data Access Bodies on procedures and formats for data access, published by the TEHDAS2 Joint Action in September 2025, specifies that personal data must be deleted from a Secure Processing Environment within six months of the expiry of the data permit, under Article 68(12) of the EHDS Regulation (TEHDAS2, 2025).

Cross-border health data exchange therefore operates under three distinct retention regimes that do not yet have a documented technical reconciliation: a ten-year retention floor for audit logs, an unbounded erasure obligation for personal data on subject request, and a six-month deletion ceiling for processed data in Secure Processing Environments. This thesis is positioned within that unresolved tension.

---

## 1.2 Problem Statement

(target: 500 words)

The European Health Data Space establishes legal rights and operational obligations, but it does not yet prescribe how the three retention regimes described above are to be reconciled in technical practice. The result is a structural conflict embedded in the cross-border audit trail.

When a Norwegian patient is treated in another Member State, the access event is logged in the local NCPeH's ATNA-compliant audit repository, retained for at least ten years, and accessible to the patient through the home country's audit-log interface (Simjanoska Misheva et al., 2025). If, during that ten-year window, the patient exercises the right to erasure under GDPR Article 17, the institution faces a choice between three positions, each of which violates one of the other regimes. Deleting the audit record honours Article 17 but destroys the integrity of the audit chain that ATNA, eIDAS-based access traceability, and EHDS patient rights all depend upon. Retaining the audit record preserves the chain but fails the erasure obligation. Pseudonymising the record creates ambiguity about whether the pseudonymisation is reversible, which under GDPR Recital 26 may not satisfy true anonymisation.

The same conflict arises in the secondary-use pathway. When a researcher receives a data permit from the Norwegian Health Data Access Body, Helsedataservice (Folkehelseinstituttet, 2024), and processes the data within a Norwegian Secure Processing Environment such as those operated by the Trusted Research Environments collaboration NORTRE (Norwegian Trusted Research Environments, 2025), the TEHDAS2 specification requires deletion of personal data from the SPE within six months of permit expiry. Yet audit records of the access, processing, and analytical operations performed inside the SPE remain subject to the ATNA ten-year minimum.

These conflicts are not theoretical. The Norwegian SPUHiN project, jointly led by Helsedirektoratet and the Norwegian Institute of Public Health, explicitly acknowledged in its November 2024 draft Recommendations for Minimum Requirements for Secure Processing Environments in Norway that the country lacks a formal regulatory definition of what constitutes a closed and secure analysis infrastructure, and that the definitional work itself remains contested (SPUHiN, 2024). Norwegian implementation of the EHDS therefore proceeds against a regulatory and technical background in which the audit-retention versus right-to-erasure question is not yet resolved.

A small but rapidly growing body of cryptographic research has begun to address adjacent problems. Albalwy (2026) demonstrates zero-knowledge policy enforcement for cross-institutional health data sharing within a single jurisdiction. Natsiavas et al. (2021) document KONFIDO, the most direct architectural ancestor for cross-border health data security, which combined trusted execution environments, homomorphic encryption, and blockchain-based auditing on the OpenNCP gateway. Bai et al. (2022) describe Health-zkIDM, a Hyperledger Fabric-based decentralised identity system for healthcare. None of these works addresses the audit-retention versus erasure tension at the cross-border audit layer.

The problem this thesis addresses is therefore the absence of a technically specified, regulation-aligned mechanism for reconciling the three retention regimes of cross-border health data audit trails under EHDS, in a manner compatible with the operational reality of Norwegian implementation.

---

## 1.3 Research Objectives and Questions

(target: 350 words)

The objective of this thesis is to specify and demonstrate a verifiable mechanism that reconciles the conflicting retention regimes identified in Section 1.2. The mechanism is termed Crypto-Erasure by Invalidation. Its design rests on a single conceptual move: rather than deleting audit records to satisfy GDPR Article 17, the cryptographic references that bind the audit record to retrievable personal data are mathematically invalidated, so that the audit chain remains intact for the ATNA ten-year minimum and for accountability purposes, but the personal data referenced from the audit record can no longer be reconstructed.

The thesis is guided by one primary research question.

**Primary research question.** How can a verifiable crypto-erasure mechanism be designed to reconcile the conflicting data-retention requirements of cross-border health data exchange under the European Health Data Space — specifically the tension between IHE ATNA's minimum ten-year audit retention, GDPR Article 17's right to erasure, and TEHDAS2's six-month Secure Processing Environment deletion rule — while preserving audit integrity in a Norwegian implementation context?

The primary question is decomposed into three sub-questions.

**SQ1.** What are the precise points of conflict between ATNA, GDPR Article 17, and TEHDAS2 deletion rules in the cross-border EHDS workflow?

**SQ2.** Can a cryptographic invalidation mechanism — where proof references are mathematically invalidated rather than data being deleted — satisfy all three constraints simultaneously?

**SQ3.** How would such a mechanism integrate with Norway's current cross-border infrastructure, specifically the NCPeH operated by Helsedirektoratet and Norsk Helsenett, the Health Data Access Body Helsedataservice, and the Secure Processing Environments operated under NORTRE?

These three sub-questions correspond to the analytical, design, and integration dimensions of the contribution. SQ1 is addressed primarily through Chapter 2's literature review and Chapter 4's design rationale. SQ2 is addressed through Chapter 4's specification and Chapter 5's sandbox demonstration. SQ3 is addressed through Chapter 4's integration analysis and Chapter 6's discussion of practical implications for Norwegian implementing actors.

---

## 1.4 Significance and Relevance

(target: 400 words)

The significance of this thesis rests on three convergent factors that make the audit-retention versus erasure question both timely and concretely Norwegian.

First, the timing is not abstract. The Group One priority categories of EHDS, comprising patient summaries and ePrescriptions, become mandatory across the EU and EEA in March 2029, with the Group Two categories of laboratory results, medical imaging, and hospital discharge reports following in March 2031 (European Commission, 2025a). The implementing acts that will specify technical detail are due by March 2027. Norway's NCPeH is in late-stage piloting, with operational rollout scheduled across 2025 and 2026 (European Commission, 2025b). Decisions about how audit trails will handle conflicting retention obligations will be made within the next twenty-four months, in a regulatory environment that does not yet have a settled answer.

Second, the Norwegian implementation context provides a concrete substrate. Norway has a defined Health Data Access Body in Helsedataservice (Folkehelseinstituttet, 2024); a developed Trusted Research Environment collaboration in NORTRE (Norwegian Trusted Research Environments, 2025); an active national policy consultation through the SPUHiN project (SPUHiN, 2024); and parallel ongoing legislative work on Pasientjournalloven and Helsepersonelloven covering professional confidentiality and cross-organisational access (Stortinget, 2025). The thesis can therefore be positioned against a real, named, currently active implementation pathway rather than against a hypothetical European deployment.

Third, the novelty positioning is defensible against current peer-reviewed literature. Albalwy (2026) addresses zero-knowledge policy enforcement for cross-institutional health data sharing within a single jurisdiction, occupying the cross-institutional space distinct from the cross-border space this thesis addresses. KONFIDO (Natsiavas et al., 2021) addressed cross-border security but did not resolve the audit-retention versus erasure tension and was hardware-dependent through its use of trusted execution environments. The 2025 research agenda for privacy-enhancing technologies under EHDS (Frontiers in Digital Health, 2025) identifies governance and technological solutions as an open category but does not specify mechanisms for the specific tension this thesis addresses.

The thesis also frames the problem as one of information logistics. The reconciliation of conflicting retention regimes across jurisdictional boundaries is structurally identical to the challenges faced by cross-border logistics under conflicting record-keeping requirements imposed by different national authorities. This framing situates the contribution within the disciplinary identity of Sustainable Energy Logistics at HiMolde, treating digital health data as a flow problem under regulatory constraint.

---

## 1.5 Scope and Out-of-Scope

(target: 350 words)

This thesis is bounded by a deliberate and explicit scope. The bounding is not a limitation to be apologised for but a methodological commitment to defensibility within the time and resources available for an MSc thesis.

**The thesis contributes a design-science specification.** It specifies the mechanism, demonstrates it through a Python-based sandbox using synthetic Synthea-generated FHIR data, and positions it within a layered compliance architecture grounded in the Norwegian implementation of EHDS. The specification and the sandbox together constitute the artefact.

The thesis explicitly does **not** include the following. First, it does not build a working zero-knowledge SNARK circuit; the cryptographic primitive that would underpin a production implementation is treated as a deferrable engineering layer and is briefly discussed in Chapter 7 as future work. Second, it does not deploy to a real National Contact Point for eHealth; integration with Norwegian NCPeH operations remains a theoretical mapping rather than a runtime test. Third, it does not conduct human-subject interviews; no clinicians, compliance officers, or patients were interviewed for this thesis, and no qualitative empirical data are reported. Fourth, it does not measure real hardware energy consumption; no claims about energy or sustainability metrics are made beyond conceptual framing. Fifth, it does not use real patient data; all data used in the sandbox are synthetic, generated by Synthea, and contain no information about real individuals. Sixth, it does not implement healthcare professional authentication mechanisms or consent propagation protocols beyond the invalidation mechanism that is the subject of the thesis. Seventh, it does not provide formal Coq or Lean proofs of the cryptographic properties of the proposed mechanism; the security argument is presented informally under standard assumptions. Eighth, it does not address non-EU and non-EEA jurisdictions.

Three components that are conceptually related to the broader research direction — a Triple-Assertion Circuit for healthcare professional authorisation, a sustainability indicator for zero-knowledge proof systems, and a cross-border consent revocation propagation protocol — are presented in a separate addendum to the thesis supervisor, signalling potential future research direction without claiming results that have not been produced.

---

## 1.6 Methodological Approach

(target: 250 words)

The thesis adopts Design Science Research, as established by Hevner, March, Park, and Ram (2004) and elaborated by Peffers, Tuunanen, Rothenberger, and Chatterjee (2007). Design Science Research is the appropriate paradigm where a research project produces an artefact intended to address a defined problem in an information-systems context, evaluates the artefact, and communicates the contribution. The framework prescribes a cycle of problem identification, definition of objectives, design and development of the artefact, demonstration, evaluation, and communication.

This thesis adopts the specification-and-demonstration variant of Design Science Research. The artefact takes the form of a mechanism specification supported by a software demonstration. The demonstration is conducted in a controlled sandbox environment using synthetic data generated by Synthea, an open-source tool for the generation of synthetic patient records compliant with HL7 FHIR R4. The choice of FHIR R4 reflects the current Norwegian basisprofiler, which is the official Norwegian national constraint set on the international FHIR R4 standard, published and maintained by HL7 Norway (HL7 Norway, 2024).

The evaluation strategy is qualitative and analytical rather than quantitative and empirical. Internal validity is assessed through logical consistency under the three retention constraints. External validity is assessed through compatibility with verified existing infrastructure. Reliability is supported through deterministic sandbox execution with fixed random seeds. No empirical performance benchmarks are reported, and no claims about latency, throughput, energy consumption, or computational cost are presented as measurement results. The full methodological treatment is provided in Chapter 3.

---

## 1.7 Thesis Structure

(target: 200 words)

The thesis is organised in seven chapters and two appendices.

**Chapter 1** introduces the regulatory background, the problem, the research objectives, the significance of the study, the scope and explicit out-of-scope boundaries, and the methodological approach.

**Chapter 2** reviews the literature in four domains: the cross-border health data exchange landscape under EHDS, the audit-retention versus right-to-erasure tension, cryptographic approaches to audit compliance, and the Norwegian secondary-use infrastructure. It identifies the conceptual gap that this thesis addresses and positions the contribution within the broader research agenda for privacy-enhancing technologies in European health data spaces.

**Chapter 3** establishes the design science research paradigm, explains the choice of the specification-and-demonstration variant, describes the synthetic data methodology and the sandbox approach, and addresses validity, reliability, and ethical considerations.

**Chapter 4** specifies the Crypto-Erasure by Invalidation mechanism, including design goals, conceptual model, architectural positioning, the invalidation registry, audit-trail behaviour, and integration analysis with Norwegian NCPeH and NORTRE infrastructure.

**Chapter 5** presents the sandbox demonstration. **Chapter 6** discusses findings and their implications for practice, theory, and policy. **Chapter 7** concludes, summarises contributions, revisits limitations, and outlines future work.

## What "depth" actually depends on

Depth in academic prose has three drivers:

1. **Word budget per claim** — more words per claim allows more nuance, more evidence, more counter-argument
2. **Citations per claim** — more sources verifying a claim makes it more defensible
3. **Attention budget** — how much of my reasoning I can spend on each section without splitting focus

3 runs vs 4 runs doesn't change drivers (1) and (2). The word budget per section stays the same (because the chapter target stays at 6,400 words). The citations stay the same (each section already has its v7 sources slotted).

What 4 runs *does* change is driver (3) — my attention budget per section. Splitting Run 2 (the citation-heaviest, most synthesis-demanding pair) into two runs gives the most depth gain. Splitting the lighter sections gains less.

# Chapter 2 — Literature Review and Theoretical Foundation

## 2.1 Review Strategy

(target 400 words)

The literature review in this chapter is structured around the conceptual architecture of the thesis rather than a comprehensive bibliographic survey. The aim is to establish, with verifiable sources, the four conditions on which the thesis contribution depends: that the cross-border health data landscape under the European Health Data Space is sufficiently advanced and Norwegian participation sufficiently committed for the contribution to be timely; that the audit-retention versus right-to-erasure tension is real, named in primary regulatory and technical sources, and not yet resolved; that cryptographic compliance approaches have advanced enough to make the proposed mechanism technically plausible while leaving the specific cross-border erasure problem unaddressed; and that the Norwegian secondary-use infrastructure provides a concrete substrate within which the contribution can be positioned.

Sources were identified through a combination of structured database searches, citation snowballing from foundational papers, and direct retrieval of primary regulatory, standards, and government documents. Peer-reviewed literature was searched in Scopus, PubMed, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, and Google Scholar, restricted to publications dated 2022 through May 2026, using combinations of the terms zero-knowledge, blockchain, health data, electronic health records, cross-border, EHDS, MyHealth@EU, GDPR Article 17, audit, erasure, crypto-shredding, and Secure Processing Environment. Primary regulatory sources, including Regulation (EU) 2025/327 establishing the European Health Data Space, the General Data Protection Regulation, and TEHDAS2 deliverables, were retrieved directly from their authoritative European Union or Joint Action repositories. Norwegian primary sources, including Helsedirektoratet's EHDS landing page, the SPUHiN minimum requirements draft, and the relevant amendments to Pasientjournalloven and Helsepersonelloven, were retrieved directly from helsedirektoratet.no, helsedata.no, and stortinget.no.

Two inclusion criteria were applied. First, every cited source must be retrievable through a public URL, a DOI, or a primary repository at the time of writing, so that examiners can independently verify any claim. Second, in cases of conflict between secondary commentary and primary regulatory text, the primary text prevails. Where secondary sources are cited, this is for analysis or interpretation rather than for the factual content of the regulation or standard itself.

The review proceeds through four substantive domains in Sections 2.2 to 2.5, develops the information-logistics framing that anchors the contribution within the Sustainable Energy Logistics discipline in Section 2.6, compares the proposed contribution against verified existing work in Section 2.7, identifies the research gap in Section 2.8, and positions the thesis contribution against that gap in Section 2.9.

## 2.2 The Cross-Border Health Data Exchange Landscape

(target 1,000 words)

The European Union's cross-border health data infrastructure rests on a regulatory framework that has matured rapidly during the past three years, and on a technical platform that has been in operation, in voluntary form, for more than a decade. The two layers are now converging under the European Health Data Space Regulation, which establishes the legal architecture within which the existing technical platform must scale.

Regulation (EU) 2025/327 of 11 February 2025 establishing the European Health Data Space entered into force on 26 March 2025, opening a multi-year transition during which Member States and European Economic Area countries must align their national infrastructures with binding Union-wide requirements (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2025). The regulation governs both primary use, meaning the use of electronic health data for the provision of healthcare to the data subject, and secondary use, meaning use for research, innovation, policy-making, regulatory activities, and public health (European Commission, 2025a). For primary use, the regulation establishes a calendar that the implementing acts must operationalise by 26 March 2027, with Group One priority categories of patient summaries and ePrescriptions becoming exchangeable across all Member States by 26 March 2029, and Group Two categories of laboratory results, medical imaging, and hospital discharge reports following by 26 March 2031 (Healthy Europe, 2026; European Commission, 2025a). Each Member State must designate a National Digital Health Authority by June 2025, and healthcare providers and electronic health record vendors must certify their systems for interoperability and security compliance by January 2026 (Ernst & Young, 2025).

The technical platform implementing cross-border primary use is MyHealth@EU, the operational successor to the eHealth Digital Service Infrastructure (eHDSI). MyHealth@EU connects national systems through National Contact Points for eHealth (NCPeH), each operated by the participating country's competent authority and funded historically through the Connecting Europe Facility Telecom Programme (2015–2020) and currently through the EU4Health Programme (2021–2027) (European Commission, 2025b). Governance is exercised by two coordinating bodies: the eHealth DSI EU countries Expert Group (eHMSEG), composed of managers responsible for NCPeH implementation in participating countries, and the eHealth Operational Management Board (eHOMB), composed of European Commission representatives and the eHMSEG Chairs (European Commission, 2025b).

The MyHealth@EU operational architecture follows a six-step transmission flow at the NCPeH gateway level, recently characterised in detail by Simjanoska Misheva et al. (2025). When a healthcare provider in a country of treatment requests cross-border data, the source country NCPeH performs service discovery to locate the patient's home country gateway; performs patient discovery against the patient's national identifier; retrieves the requested document, typically an International Patient Summary or an ePrescription, in the source country's native clinical document format; transforms it through a pivot transformer that converts national clinical document representations to the common European Electronic Health Record Exchange Format using SNOMED CT, LOINC, and other terminology bindings; applies the security and consent module, which validates the requesting clinician's eIDAS identity token and applies XACML-based consent policies; and finally logs the transaction in an IHE Audit Trail and Node Authentication compliant audit repository with a minimum ten-year retention period.

Norway's integration with MyHealth@EU is being implemented through a project that began in January 2023 under the joint operational responsibility of Helsedirektoratet and Norsk Helsenett SF, the national operator of the closed Norwegian health network. Norway is scheduled for go-live piloting in 2025 alongside Austria, Cyprus, Denmark, Hungary, Iceland, Italy, Romania, Slovenia, and Sweden (European Commission, 2025c). Because Norway is a member of the European Economic Area rather than of the European Union, the EHDS Regulation does not apply directly but is being processed for incorporation through the EEA Joint Committee. The Norwegian Directorate of Health delivered its formal EHDS impact and gap analysis on 11 April 2025, identifying the principal areas in which Norwegian law and infrastructure will require alignment (Helsedirektoratet, 2025a).

Parallel to the primary-use track, the regulation establishes a secondary-use track through which national Health Data Access Bodies coordinate access to electronic health data for research, innovation, and policy purposes. The interconnecting infrastructure for secondary use is HealthData@EU, which complements MyHealth@EU and operates under different technical and governance arrangements. The technical, functional, and security specifications for the Secure Processing Environments through which secondary-use data must be processed are being developed under the TEHDAS2 Joint Action, a coordinated effort of twenty-nine countries running until December 2026 (Healthy Europe, 2026). The Norwegian Health Data Access Body designated under this regime is Helsedataservice, hosted at the Folkehelseinstituttet (Norwegian Institute of Public Health), which since 2023 has held the decision-making authority for eleven statutory national health registries (Folkehelseinstituttet, 2024).

The historical context of these institutional arrangements is important for the present thesis. The Norwegian central analytics platform Helseanalyseplattformen was paused in December 2021 following legal challenges related to the Schrems II judgment on transatlantic data transfers, and was formally avviklet by the Ministry of Health and Care Services in February 2023. The Direktoratet for e-helse, which had led much of the early national e-health standards work, was itself dissolved in May 2023, with its core functions absorbed into Helsedirektoratet from 2024 onwards (Helsedirektoratet, 2023). The Norwegian secondary-use infrastructure that the EHDS will be implemented against is therefore not a centralised analytic platform but a distributed model resting on the three university-based trusted research environments — TSD at the University of Oslo, SAFE at the University of Bergen, and HUNT Cloud at NTNU — coordinated through the NORTRE collaboration (Norwegian Trusted Research Environments, 2025).

The cross-border landscape is therefore mature in its regulatory architecture, advancing in its technical infrastructure, and concretely defined in its Norwegian implementation. It is against this landscape that the audit-retention and erasure tensions become not abstract but operationally consequential, as Section 2.3 will demonstrate.

# Chapter 2 — Literature Review and Theoretical Foundation (continued)

## 2.3 The Audit-Retention vs Right-to-Erasure Tension

(target 1,200 words)

The thesis is built around a specific structural tension between three retention regimes that operate concurrently on the same cross-border health data event. Each regime is grounded in primary sources — a technical integration profile, a binding regulation, and an evolving Joint Action specification. None resolves the others. This section examines each regime in turn, then characterises the resulting conflict and the policy commentary that has begun to surface around it.

The first regime is technical. The IHE Audit Trail and Node Authentication (ATNA) profile, maintained in Volume 1 Chapter 9 of the IHE IT Infrastructure Technical Framework, specifies the foundational audit and security requirements for nodes participating in interoperable health information exchange (IHE International, 2024). ATNA establishes a Basic Secure Node that must authenticate other nodes, encrypt communications using TLS, log triggered events such as queries, views, additions, deletions, and changes within the security domain, and transmit those audit records to an Audit Record Repository. The IHE specification itself does not mandate a single global retention period, leaving that decision to the realm-specific or domain-specific deployment binding. The eHDSI security framework that operationalises ATNA within the MyHealth@EU infrastructure does specify retention in concrete terms. The framework adopted by the eHMSEG governance body for cross-border NCPeH operations requires audit repositories to retain records for a minimum of ten years, characterised by Simjanoska Misheva et al. (2025) as the binding deployment baseline. This retention floor exists because cross-border audit records support not only patient-facing access logs but also accountability for the eIDAS-based authentication of the requesting clinician, the consent validation step, and the audit trail required under the European Health Data Space patient-rights provisions.

The second regime is legal. Article 17 of the General Data Protection Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2016/679) establishes the data subject's right to obtain from the controller the erasure of personal data concerning them without undue delay, where one of the conditions in Article 17(1) applies (European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2016). These conditions include the cessation of the original purpose, the withdrawal of consent without an alternative legal basis, an objection under Article 21 with no overriding legitimate interest, and unlawful processing. The data controller bears an independent obligation to erase in these conditions, irrespective of whether the data subject has formally exercised the right (European Data Protection Board, 2026). Article 17(3) provides limited exemptions, of which two are directly relevant to the cross-border audit context. Article 17(3)(b) permits the controller to refuse erasure where processing is necessary for compliance with a legal obligation imposed by Union or Member State law. Article 17(3)(d) permits refusal where processing is necessary for scientific or historical research purposes or statistical purposes, in so far as erasure is likely to render impossible or seriously impair the achievement of those purposes. The European Data Protection Board's Coordinated Enforcement Framework report on Article 17, published on 18 February 2026 following an investigation involving 32 supervisory authorities and 764 controllers, identified the implementation of retention periods as one of five recurring issues, recommending further practical guidance on how to define and implement retention periods consistent with national legal obligations (European Data Protection Board, 2026; Matheson, 2026).

The third regime is operational and emerging. The TEHDAS2 Joint Action's draft Guideline for Health Data Access Bodies on procedures and formats for data access, published in September 2025, specifies that personal data must be deleted from a Secure Processing Environment within six months of the expiry of the data permit, under Article 68(12) of the European Health Data Space Regulation (TEHDAS2, 2025; European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2025). This is a ceiling rather than a floor. After the six-month window, only anonymised analytical results may continue to exist outside the Secure Processing Environment, and personal data are not permitted to remain. The same TEHDAS2 deliverable specifies a five-phase user journey for data access that ends in a deletion event marking the closure of the permitted processing.

The conflict is structural and operational. When a Norwegian patient is treated under MyHealth@EU in another Member State, the cross-border access event is logged in the foreign NCPeH's ATNA-compliant audit repository for at least ten years. During that window, the patient retains the right to request erasure of personal data under Article 17. If the erasure request is granted, the audit record loses its referential integrity: it points to data that no longer exist. If the erasure request is refused on Article 17(3)(b) grounds, the controller must demonstrate that the retention is genuinely necessary for compliance with a specific legal obligation, which is the recommendation the European Data Protection Board made in February 2026 (Matheson, 2026). When the same patient's data move through the secondary-use pathway and reach a Norwegian Secure Processing Environment under a Helsedataservice permit, the TEHDAS2 six-month deletion rule applies. Yet the audit records of the access, processing, and analytical operations performed inside the Secure Processing Environment remain subject to the same eHDSI ten-year baseline through the cross-border audit chain that initiated the secondary-use request.

A direct technical solution to this tension exists in the literature on cryptographic erasure, though its application to the cross-border health audit problem has not been systematically developed. The National Institute of Standards and Technology's Special Publication 800-88 Revision 2 recognises cryptographic erasure as a purge-grade sanitization technique, in which the encryption key used to protect the data is irreversibly destroyed while the encrypted data remain on the storage medium (National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2024). The European Union Agency for Cybersecurity and several national data protection authorities have begun to recognise cryptographic erasure as a means of satisfying Article 17 in distributed cloud environments, on the condition that key management is auditable and that the keys are demonstrably and irreversibly destroyed (Oneuptime, 2026). The technique is not without criticism. SecuPi (2025) argues that cryptographic erasure introduces operational complexity in row-level encryption scenarios and that auditable key management adds rather than removes overhead, making it inappropriate as a general solution for the right to erasure in heavily distributed systems. Engaging with this critique is essential for the thesis to remain defensible; Chapter 6 returns to it explicitly.

What does not yet exist in the literature, and what this thesis addresses, is the specific design of a verifiable invalidation mechanism that operates at the cross-border audit-trail boundary defined by ATNA, the eHDSI ten-year retention baseline, GDPR Article 17(3)(b), and the TEHDAS2 six-month rule, in a manner that is both technically demonstrable and compatible with the operational reality of Norwegian NCPeH and Helsedataservice. The next section reviews the cryptographic literature that informs the design of such a mechanism.

# Chapter 2 — Literature Review and Theoretical Foundation (continued)

## 2.4 Cryptographic Approaches to Audit Compliance

(target 1,200 words)

A growing body of cryptographic and systems research has developed mechanisms that address parts of the audit-compliance problem in cross-border and multi-institutional health data settings. The four most relevant strands are trusted-execution-environment-based architectures applied to OpenNCP, blockchain-based audit logging adapted to healthcare, zero-knowledge proofs applied to electronic health records and decentralised identity, and the underlying cryptographic primitives of commitment schemes and accumulators that make revocation mathematically tractable. This section reviews each strand in turn, identifying both what each contributes and what each leaves unaddressed for the specific cross-border erasure problem this thesis examines.

The KONFIDO project, funded under the Horizon 2020 programme between 2016 and 2019, remains the most directly relevant architectural ancestor for the present work. KONFIDO extended the OpenNCP cross-border health data exchange platform with a holistic security toolkit organised around four technical pillars: photonic Physical Unclonable Functions for hardware-rooted identity, homomorphic encryption for computation on encrypted patient summaries, a Security Information and Event Management system for distributed monitoring, and a blockchain-based auditing component for cross-border traceability and liability support (Diamantopoulos et al., 2019; Staffa et al., 2018). KONFIDO was piloted in Denmark, Italy, and Spain, and the lessons-learned synthesis published by Natsiavas et al. (2021) documented both the technical achievements and the substantive gaps in scaling the approach. Two of those gaps are directly relevant. First, the KONFIDO security architecture relied on Intel Software Guard Extensions trusted execution environments, creating a hardware dependency that complicates broad NCPeH deployment across heterogeneous Member State infrastructures. Second, KONFIDO's blockchain auditing component, designated as a "disruptive logging" mechanism in the project documentation, provided immutable traceability but did not engage the General Data Protection Regulation's right to erasure as a design constraint. The audit chain was treated as a feature whose value derived from its immutability, with the conflict between immutability and erasure left unresolved.

A second strand of work has explored zero-knowledge proofs applied to electronic health record access control, with the most direct comparator for the present thesis being Albalwy (2026). The ZK-EHR framework uses a Groth16 zk-SNARK circuit to enforce policy compliance for cross-institutional health data sharing, with three actor roles defined as the Patient as data owner, the Doctor as care provider, and the Researcher as authorised analyst. Encrypted records are stored on the InterPlanetary File System, with on-chain smart contracts handling policy enforcement and cryptographic verification. The architecture decouples authorisation from identity disclosure, allowing a requesting actor to prove they hold valid policy-compliant credentials without revealing their identity, role, or affiliations. The framework reports an on-chain verification latency of approximately 390 milliseconds and a gas consumption of 216,631 units per verification. Albalwy's contribution occupies the cross-institutional space within a single jurisdiction; the cross-border space addressed by MyHealth@EU, with its eIDAS-based authentication chains and its operational coupling to ATNA-compliant audit repositories spanning multiple national legal regimes, is genuinely distinct.

The Health-zkIDM system developed by Bai et al. (2022) provides a complementary perspective. Built on Hyperledger Fabric with zero-knowledge proof components implemented at the chaincode level, Health-zkIDM achieves throughput exceeding 400 transactions per second in Caliper benchmarking, demonstrating that decentralised identity management with cryptographic privacy guarantees is operationally viable in healthcare settings. The architecture targets identity verification rather than audit-trail erasure, but its performance evidence is informative for the design constraints of any cross-border verifiable compliance mechanism.

A more recent contribution is zkFL-Health (Sharma et al., 2025), which combines federated learning with zero-knowledge proofs and trusted execution environments for medical artificial intelligence training. Clients train locally and commit cryptographic representations of their updates; an aggregator operating within a trusted execution environment computes the global update and produces a succinct zero-knowledge proof, generated using Halo2 or Nova, that the aggregation used exactly the committed inputs and applied the prescribed rule, without revealing any individual client update. Verifier nodes record cryptographic commitments on-chain, creating what the authors explicitly characterise as an "immutable audit trail" removing the need to trust any single party. zkFL-Health is significant for the present thesis in two respects: it demonstrates that the combination of trusted execution environments and zero-knowledge proofs can produce verifiable audit trails compatible with healthcare data, and it provides a recent illustration of the design pattern where commitments on-chain reference data held off-chain — a pattern central to the cryptographic-erasure-by-invalidation mechanism this thesis proposes.

Within the Norwegian clinical context, the NewbornTime project provides a deployed precedent. Brunner et al. (2025) document the deployment of a Hyperledger-based digital consent platform at Stavanger University Hospital, used between November 2021 and June 2025 in the collection of 1,012 thermal videos of newborn resuscitation events. The platform stores consent status immutably on-chain while keeping personal data encrypted and off-chain, providing a protected API for authorised retrieval and a documented General Data Protection Regulation-compliant withdrawal mechanism. The clinical viability of blockchain-anchored consent infrastructure in a Norwegian regulated healthcare setting is therefore established, although the system addresses consent recording rather than the audit-trail erasure problem.

A fourth strand of work, less visible in the healthcare literature but foundational to the design of any verifiable invalidation mechanism, is the cryptographic accumulator and commitment scheme literature. Benaloh and de Mare (1993) introduced one-way accumulators as a means of accumulating elements from a finite set into a single short value supporting membership testing. Camenisch and Lysyanskaya (2002) extended this work to dynamic accumulators with efficient revocation of anonymous credentials, providing the mathematical machinery for verifiable membership and non-membership proofs in sets that change over time. Ren (2022) surveys the field, covering applications ranging from anonymous credentials and certificate revocation through to blockchain-based audit systems. The Blockchain-based Efficient Audit Trail System proposed by ResearchGate-indexed work in 2024 applies cryptographic accumulators directly to the problem of verifying specific transaction information within a blockchain audit trail without exhaustive search, demonstrating the operational viability of accumulator-based audit verification.

Three observations emerge from this survey. First, the technical components required for a verifiable cryptographic-erasure mechanism for cross-border health audit trails exist in mature form: trusted execution environments at the OpenNCP layer (KONFIDO), zero-knowledge proof systems applied to healthcare (Albalwy 2026, Health-zkIDM, zkFL-Health), blockchain-anchored consent and audit infrastructures with Norwegian clinical validation (NewbornTime), and cryptographic accumulators with revocation semantics (Camenisch and Lysyanskaya 2002 and the subsequent literature). Second, none of these works combines these components to address the specific tension between ATNA-mandated audit retention, GDPR Article 17 erasure rights, and TEHDAS2 Secure Processing Environment deletion in the cross-border European context. Third, the broader policy literature on privacy-enhancing technologies under the European Health Data Space, including the research agenda published in Frontiers in Digital Health (2025), explicitly identifies this kind of governance-and-technology integration as an open research category. The contribution of this thesis is positioned at that named gap.

# Chapter 2 — Literature Review and Theoretical Foundation (continued)

## 2.5 Norwegian Secondary-Use Infrastructure

(target 800 words)

Norway's secondary-use infrastructure for health data is the substrate against which the European Health Data Space will be implemented at the national level. The infrastructure has three layers: a governance and access-decision layer through Helsedataservice, a data-custodian layer through the major registry holders, and an analytical-processing layer through a fragmented set of Secure Processing Environments coordinated through the NORTRE collaboration. Each layer presents a distinct compliance surface, and each interacts directly with the audit-retention versus erasure tension developed in Section 2.3.

Helsedataservice is the Norwegian Health Data Access Body designated under the emerging European Health Data Space governance architecture. It took on its current authority on 15 March 2023, when the Norwegian Directorate of Health and the Regional Committees for Medical and Health Research Ethics transferred decision-making authority over data access from eleven central health registries to Helsedataservice (Forskningsetikk, 2023). The transfer was implemented under the Regulations on national solutions for making health data available, which operationalised the statutory changes introduced in Prop. 63 L on amendments to the Health Registries Act (Helse- og omsorgsdepartementet, 2020). Applications are submitted via the helsedata.no portal, and Helsedataservice registers each application and forwards it to the relevant data custodian. The custodians for the eleven registries include the Norwegian Institute of Public Health, the Norwegian Directorate of Health, and the Norwegian Cancer Registry (Helsedataservice, 2024). The custodians then process the application and decide on access, while Helsedataservice handles the administrative gateway. Helsedataservice charges separately for case processing, and the data holders charge for data preparation and extraction, creating a two-stage cost structure that mirrors the two-stage decision structure (Helsedataservice, 2024).

The registry layer that Helsedataservice now governs includes the Norwegian Patient Registry (NPR), the Norwegian Cause of Death Registry, the Medical Birth Registry of Norway, the Norwegian Immunisation Registry (SYSVAK), the Norwegian Cardiovascular Disease Registry, the Norwegian Prescription Registry, the Norwegian Registry for Primary Health Care (KPR), the Norwegian Health Archives Registry, and several other statutory registries (Folkehelseinstituttet, 2024). Together these registries cover effectively the entire Norwegian population and can be linked through the national identification number, providing a population-scale data resource for research, public health, and policy that is structurally similar in scope and depth to the Finnish registry system and distinct from the more fragmented data landscapes of larger European Union Member States.

The Secure Processing Environment layer is where the operational reconciliation of EHDS Article 73 with Norwegian implementation must occur, and where the structural fragility of the current arrangements is most visible. The SPUHiN minimum requirements draft of November 2024 documents the actual state of Norwegian SPE practice in a passage worth quoting at length, because it determines the design space within which any cryptographic compliance mechanism for Norwegian SPEs must operate. Based on the descriptions provided by applicants in their permit applications to Helsedataservice during 2023, the SPUHiN drafting team observed that, "it is however most common to use either an analysis infrastructure currently available from the universities... or some type of server, database, folder, area or zone most likely provided by the data controller's own IT provider. A few also refer to OneDrive, Office365, disconnected PC or a partner in another country" (SPUHiN, 2024, p. 4). This passage makes explicit that the Norwegian SPE landscape is not merely distributed across the three NORTRE university nodes but is operationally fragmented, with substantial volumes of secondary-use processing occurring outside the NORTRE substrate altogether.

The three primary NORTRE nodes — TSD at the University of Oslo (operational since 2012), SAFE at the University of Bergen (operational since 2015), and HUNT Cloud at the NTNU (operational since 2013) — provide infrastructure that meets the European Open Science Cloud trusted research environment standards and that is connected through the EOSC-ENTRUST blueprint project to a federated European network (Norwegian Trusted Research Environments, 2025). The SPUHiN draft establishes that these infrastructures will form the operational base of EHDS-compliant secondary use in Norway, but the explicit acknowledgment that some processing already occurs outside this infrastructure, including on disconnected PCs or on infrastructure provided by partners in other countries, signals the scope of the policy and technical work that will be required to bring Norwegian secondary use into formal alignment with Article 73 by the EHDS deadlines.

The thesis's contribution must be designed against this operational reality. A verifiable cryptographic-erasure mechanism that assumes a clean, homogeneous SPE substrate will fail in implementation. A mechanism that operates at the boundary between the audit trail and the data references, and that can be deployed regardless of whether the processing occurs in TSD, SAFE, HUNT Cloud, or on a more fragmented institutional infrastructure, will fit the actual Norwegian context.

## 2.6 Information Logistics Framing

(target 600 words)

The thesis frames the audit-retention versus erasure problem as one of information logistics. This framing is not a metaphor but an analytical commitment that grounds the contribution within the disciplinary identity of Sustainable Energy Logistics at HiMolde and within an active academic literature on cross-border data movement under regulatory constraint.

The International Chamber of Commerce (2025) policy brief on data flows in supply chains documents that cross-border data flows are functionally equivalent to material flows in their structural role within global supply chain operations. They enable real-time coordination, traceability, customs clearance, and the deployment of digital tools across jurisdictional boundaries. They are also subject to the same kind of fragmented regulatory landscape that has historically constrained physical cross-border logistics through divergent national rules. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development has estimated that full data autarky, defined as complete restriction of cross-border data flows, would reduce global gross domestic product by 4.5 percent and cut exports by 8.5 percent (International Chamber of Commerce, 2025). Restrictive and fragmented data policies act as non-tariff barriers in the same operational sense that documentation requirements, retention obligations, and audit rules act as non-tariff barriers in physical logistics.

The structural analogy is precise rather than loose. A Norwegian patient summary moving from a Norwegian National Contact Point for eHealth to a Spanish point of care is a digital good crossing a jurisdictional boundary. It must satisfy the originating jurisdiction's audit and retention rules, the destination jurisdiction's clinical and consent rules, and any superordinate Union-level provisions. The audit log of the cross-border access event is the digital equivalent of the customs documentation that accompanies physical goods. The ten-year retention floor for that audit log under the eHDSI security framework is the digital equivalent of mandatory customs record-keeping obligations under physical trade law. The right to erasure under General Data Protection Regulation Article 17 is the digital equivalent of the destruction-of-records requirements that apply to perishable or sensitive physical goods. The conflict between these regimes is the same kind of conflict that physical logistics has long managed through ledger-based reconciliation systems, certified destruction protocols, and chain-of-custody documentation.

The maritime sector provides a concrete Norwegian-context illustration of the information-logistics framing in operation. Norwegian regulations on the medical examination of seafarers, governed by the Norwegian Maritime Authority under the implementation of the International Convention on Standards of Training, Certification and Watchkeeping for Seafarers and the Maritime Labour Convention 2006, were amended specifically to implement the General Data Protection Regulation, restricting electronic registration of medical certificates by seafarer's doctors operating outside Norway and the European Economic Area (Norwegian Maritime Authority, 2023). The amendments demonstrate that cross-border health data flow is not a theoretical question for Norwegian maritime and offshore logistics; it is an operationally binding regulatory constraint that already shapes which doctors can submit which medical certifications electronically and which cannot.

A small but technically substantial literature has begun to address cross-border data flow compliance as a logistics and supply chain problem in its own right. Zhuang et al. (2024) propose a Compliance Management System for Cross-Border Data Transfer that integrates multiple legal frameworks into a unified real-time compliance engine, demonstrating that the operational complexity of cross-border data flow under fragmented regulatory regimes is sufficient to warrant a dedicated system-engineering response. The present thesis sits within this emerging literature, contributing a specific mechanism for the audit-retention component of the broader cross-border health data flow problem.

## 2.7 Comparative Analysis

(target 600 words)

The position of the proposed contribution within the existing literature is summarised in Table 2.1, which compares VERA-SNARK against the most directly relevant comparator systems on five dimensions: the scope of cross-border versus cross-institutional operation, the dependency on hardware-rooted trust, the engagement with the GDPR right to erasure as a design constraint, the targeting of primary use versus secondary use under the European Health Data Space, and the grounding in Norwegian operational context.

**Table 2.1 — Comparative Analysis of Cryptographic Compliance Approaches to Health Data Audit**

| System | Cross-Border or Cross-Institutional | Hardware Dependency | Addresses GDPR Article 17 Erasure | Primary or Secondary Use | Norwegian Context |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| KONFIDO (Natsiavas et al., 2021; Diamantopoulos et al., 2019) | Cross-border (OpenNCP) | Yes — Intel SGX | No — treats immutability as feature | Primary use | EU pilot (Denmark, Italy, Spain); not Norway-specific |
| ZK-EHR (Albalwy, 2026) | Cross-institutional | No — software only | Partial — addresses revocation, not audit-retention conflict | Primary use (clinical) | None |
| Health-zkIDM (Bai et al., 2022) | Identity (institutional) | No | No | Primary use (identity) | None |
| zkFL-Health (Sharma et al., 2025) | Cross-institutional federated | Yes — TEE for aggregator confidentiality | No | Secondary use (AI training) | None |
| NewbornTime (Brunner et al., 2025) | Single-institution (Stavanger) | No | Yes — GDPR-compliant consent withdrawal | Primary use (clinical research) | Yes — Norwegian deployment |
| SPUHiN minimum requirements (SPUHiN, 2024) | National policy framework | n/a — specification | Acknowledged but unresolved | Secondary use (SPE) | Yes — Norwegian policy |
| **VERA-SNARK (this thesis)** | **Cross-border** | **No — software only** | **Yes — by design** | **Both, focused on audit-trail boundary** | **Yes — designed against Norwegian substrate** |

The table makes explicit that no existing comparator combines the five characteristics that define the contribution space of this thesis: cross-border operation, software-only deployment, explicit engagement with the audit-retention versus erasure tension, applicability across both primary and secondary use through the cross-border audit trail, and grounding in Norwegian operational reality. KONFIDO is the closest architectural ancestor on the cross-border dimension but is hardware-dependent and does not address erasure. ZK-EHR and Health-zkIDM are software-only but operate cross-institutionally rather than cross-border. zkFL-Health uses a hybrid TEE-plus-ZK architecture but addresses a different use case in medical AI training. NewbornTime engages erasure but is single-institution. The SPUHiN minimum requirements draft addresses the Norwegian policy substrate but is a specification framework rather than a mechanism.

The thesis does not claim that VERA-SNARK invents zero-knowledge proofs, cryptographic erasure, or distributed audit logging. Each of these primitives exists in mature form, with citations established in Sections 2.3 and 2.4. The contribution is the combination of these primitives into a specific mechanism that addresses a named gap in the comparator landscape. The novelty claim is therefore an *application novelty* — bringing an established technique into a specific operational context where it has not been combined and demonstrated for that context — rather than a *foundational novelty* claim about cryptographic primitives.

This positioning is methodologically and academically defensible. Design science research recognises application contributions as a legitimate category, particularly where the application demonstrates the technique in a domain where its non-trivial integration with existing infrastructure has not previously been worked out. Sections 2.8 and 2.9 develop the specific gap statement and the thesis positioning that result from this comparative analysis.

## 2.8 Identified Research Gaps

(target 400 words)

The literature reviewed in this chapter establishes three specific gaps that motivate the thesis contribution.

The first gap is technical-operational. No existing framework provides a mechanism for reconciling the three distinct retention regimes that operate concurrently on cross-border health data under the European Health Data Space: the IHE ATNA-based ten-year minimum audit retention required under the eHDSI security framework that operationalises MyHealth@EU, the GDPR Article 17 right to erasure with its Article 17(3) exemptions, and the TEHDAS2 six-month Secure Processing Environment deletion rule under EHDS Article 68(12). The European Data Protection Board's February 2026 Coordinated Enforcement Framework report explicitly identifies the implementation of retention periods as a recurring issue across 32 supervisory authorities and 764 controllers and recommends further practical guidance, indicating that the gap is recognised at the regulatory level.

The second gap is application-specific. The cryptographic primitives required to address the retention conflict — cryptographic erasure as recognised in NIST Special Publication 800-88 Revision 2, dynamic cryptographic accumulators with efficient revocation as established by Camenisch and Lysyanskaya (2002), zero-knowledge proof systems applied to healthcare data sharing as demonstrated by Albalwy (2026) and others, and blockchain-anchored audit infrastructures with clinical Norwegian deployment as demonstrated by the NewbornTime project — exist in mature form. None has been integrated into a mechanism specifically designed for the cross-border European Health Data Space audit trail, applied across both the primary-use NCPeH layer and the secondary-use Helsedataservice and NORTRE Secure Processing Environment layer, and demonstrated against synthetic data representative of Norwegian implementation conditions.

The third gap is contextual. The Norwegian operational reality, documented in the SPUHiN November 2024 minimum requirements draft, includes a substantial fraction of secondary-use processing that occurs outside the NORTRE substrate on infrastructure that ranges from individual data controllers' IT systems to consumer cloud services and disconnected personal computers. A compliance mechanism designed for an idealised SPE substrate will fail in this operational context. A mechanism designed at the audit-trail boundary, operating regardless of where the underlying processing occurs, can address the fragmented operational reality that the Norwegian Directorate of Health and Norwegian Institute of Public Health have themselves documented.

These three gaps converge on a single research question, addressed by the thesis through the specification and demonstration of a verifiable crypto-erasure mechanism designed for the cross-border audit trail under the European Health Data Space, in the Norwegian implementation context.

## 2.9 Conceptual Positioning of the Thesis

(target 200 words)

The contribution of this thesis is positioned at the intersection of the three identified gaps. The mechanism specified in Chapter 4, demonstrated in Chapter 5, and discussed against the comparator landscape in Chapter 6 is termed Crypto-Erasure by Invalidation. It operates at the audit-trail boundary defined by the IHE Audit Trail and Node Authentication profile as deployed in the eHDSI security framework, applies the recognised cryptographic-erasure technique from NIST Special Publication 800-88 Revision 2 to that boundary, uses cryptographic commitment and accumulator primitives from the established literature to make invalidation verifiable, and is designed against the Norwegian operational substrate documented in the SPUHiN minimum requirements draft and the Helsedataservice workflow.

The thesis does not claim that any individual cryptographic primitive is novel. It claims that the integration of these primitives into a specified mechanism for the cross-border audit-retention versus right-to-erasure problem under the European Health Data Space, designed against the operational reality of Norwegian secondary-use infrastructure, is novel. The remaining chapters elaborate this claim through the design science research methodology established in Chapter 3 and applied through Chapter 4 specification and Chapter 5 demonstration.

## The classification problem

Looking at what we have:

| Source | Type | Where it currently lives |
|---|---|---|
| EHDS Regulation 2025/327 | Primary regulatory | Subsheet 4 (Regulations & Standards Tracker) |
| NIST SP 800-88 Rev.2 | Primary technical standard | Subsheet 6 (Technical Standards Inventory) — OR Subsheet 4 |
| Albalwy 2026 MDPI Systems | Peer-reviewed academic | Subsheet 1 (Scopus and Database) |
| Helsedirektoratet EHDS page | Norwegian government primary | Subsheet 12 (Norwegian Primary Sources Tracker) |
| ICC Data Flows brief 2025 | Policy primary | **No clear home** |
| EY commentary on EHDS implementation calendar | Secondary legal commentary | **No clear home** |
| Matheson commentary on EDPB CEF report | Secondary legal commentary | **No clear home** |
| SecuPi blog "Crypto-Shredding NOT Nirvana" | Industry critical commentary | **No clear home** |
| Healthy Europe implementation tracking | Implementation news | **No clear home** |

Right now I dumped all five "no clear home" sources into Subsheet 1 (Scopus and Database) as POLICY-001 through POLICY-005. That is wrong. Subsheet 1's name is *Scopus and Database* — it implies peer-reviewed indexed sources. Putting industry blogs and law-firm commentary there inflates the apparent quality of the literature corpus and confuses anyone reviewing the substrate (including future Tiger).

## Three options, ranked

### Option A — Create a dedicated Subsheet 19: Secondary and Policy Sources Tracker

**Best option.** Clean separation by source quality. Examiners (and you) can see at a glance which citations are peer-reviewed academic vs which are policy briefs vs which are industry commentary.

The schema would be:

`Source ID | Title | Author/Organisation | Year | Type (policy brief / law-firm commentary / industry analysis / regulatory authority interpretation / news tracking) | Issuing Body | URL | Date Retrieved | Quality Tier (T1 primary policy / T2 reputable secondary / T3 industry commentary) | Used For (Section reference) | Why Cited (1 sentence) | Risk if Source Disappears (Y/N) | Replacement Strategy | Flag | Flag-Date | Flag-Note | Verification-Trail`

Then move POLICY-001 through POLICY-005 from Subsheet 1 into Subsheet 19. Subsheet 1 returns to being a clean academic-only registry.

**Pros:**
- Clean classification by source type
- Examiner can immediately see the academic vs policy ratio of citations
- Makes it visible where the thesis relies on industry commentary (which signals where you are most vulnerable in viva)
- Forces explicit tier ranking — pushes you to ask "do I really need this T3 source, or can I find a T1/T2 equivalent?"
- The "Risk if Source Disappears" column is important: industry blogs disappear; the SecuPi link could 404 in a year. The column forces a backup plan.

**Cons:**
- One more subsheet to maintain (18 → 19 → 20 if Citation Ledger also lands)
- Small overhead at creation

### Option B — Add a "Tier" column to Subsheet 1

Keep everything in Subsheet 1 (Scopus and Database) but add a Tier column: T1 (primary regulatory / primary technical standard / peer-reviewed academic) vs T2 (reputable secondary) vs T3 (industry commentary).

**Pros:**
- No new subsheet
- Single source of truth for all citations

**Cons:**
- Subsheet 1's name is still "Scopus and Database" — misnames what is in it
- Industry blogs sit in the same tab as Camenisch & Lysyanskaya 2002 CRYPTO paper — same visual weight, different epistemic weight
- Less defensible if examiner reviews the substrate

### Option C — Split secondary commentary into Subsheet 14 (External Document Audit Log)

Subsheet 14 already exists as the audit log for external documents (the GPT-doc analyses you sent me, etc). It could absorb policy briefs and commentary.

**Pros:**
- Reuses an existing tab

**Cons:**
- Subsheet 14's purpose is auditing *third-party analytical documents* (GPT-A, GPT-B, GPT-C summaries). Policy briefs and law-firm commentary are different category — they are *citable sources*, not documents-being-audited. Conflating these confuses both purposes.
- This option is wrong on category grounds.

## My honest recommendation

**Option A — Create Subsheet 19: Secondary and Policy Sources Tracker.**

The reason is honesty in the substrate. When you sit down for viva and an examiner asks "what is your strongest evidence for the audit-retention versus erasure conflict?" — you need to be able to answer instantly: "the EDPB Coordinated Enforcement Framework report from February 2026 (T1 primary regulatory), supported by the Matheson legal commentary (T2) and the SecuPi critical industry view that I engage as a counter-position (T3)."

That answer is only possible if your substrate makes the tiering visible.

## What I propose

Let me produce the patch for Subsheet 19 now, and move POLICY-001 through POLICY-005 into it cleanly. This takes 5 minutes and improves the substrate hygiene before Chapter 3 starts.

# PROPOSED PATCH — Create Subsheet 19: Secondary and Policy Sources Tracker

## Tab name

**Subsheet 19: Secondary and Policy Sources Tracker**

## Header schema

`Source ID | Title | Author/Organisation | Year | Type | Issuing Body | URL | Date Retrieved | Quality Tier | Used For (Chapter.Section) | Why Cited | Risk if Source Disappears | Replacement Strategy | Flag | Flag-Date | Flag-Note | Verification-Trail`

## Tier definitions (for the Quality Tier column)

- **T1 — Primary policy / regulatory authority interpretation**: documents issued by intergovernmental bodies (ICC, OECD, UN), EU regulatory authorities (EDPB official reports), or recognised national authorities acting in policy-issuing capacity
- **T2 — Reputable secondary commentary**: law-firm analyses, established think-tank reports, academic-affiliated commentary, established journalism with named authors and verifiable expertise

# Novelty Audit — Honest Verdict

## The direct answer to your question

**Do we have a defensible novelty yet? Partially. It is not yet at the depth that makes the thesis genuinely valuable. Here is exactly where it stands.**

## What our current contribution actually is

Stripped of framing, the thesis currently claims:

> *Apply the known technique of cryptographic erasure (NIST SP 800-88) plus known accumulator primitives (Camenisch-Lysyanskaya) to the known conflict between ATNA retention, GDPR Art 17, and TEHDAS2 deletion, in the Norwegian EHDS context, demonstrated on a Synthea sandbox.*

That is an **application contribution**. It is real. It is defensible at MSc level. But let me be clinical about its weaknesses, because you asked me not to flatter.

## The three honest problems with our novelty

**Problem 1 — The conflict we "discovered" is already named.**
During Run 2 I found the Axiom blog ("Right To Be Forgotten vs Audit Trail Mandates") and the SecuPi critique. The EDPB CEF report (Feb 2026) explicitly names retention-period implementation as a recurring issue. So the *tension* is not novel. It is recognised. We are not the first to see it. We are at best the first to propose this specific reconciliation mechanism for this specific cross-border EHDS pathway. That is narrower than it sounds.

**Problem 2 — The mechanism may not be novel either.**
Crypto-shredding to satisfy GDPR Art 17 while retaining encrypted records is already documented practice (Oneuptime, NIST). The question a sharp examiner asks: *"What does invalidation-by-accumulator add over standard crypto-shredding that the literature already describes?"* Right now we do not have a crisp answer. If the answer is "we apply it to audit trails specifically," that is thin.

**Problem 3 — A demonstration is not a finding.**
The Synthea sandbox shows the mechanism *runs*. It does not show it is *better*, *necessary*, or *correct under adversarial conditions*. A demonstration that something works as designed is the weakest form of evaluation. It answers "can this be built" not "does this matter."

## Where genuine, defensible novelty actually lives

Looking across the whole substrate, the deepest defensible novelty is **not** the crypto-erasure mechanism itself. It is one of these, in order of strength:

**Candidate 1 — The formal characterisation of the three-regime conflict (strongest).**
Nobody in the verified literature has *formally modelled* the tri-lateral constraint: ATNA 10-yr floor ∧ GDPR Art 17 erasure ∧ TEHDAS2 6-month ceiling, as a single constraint-satisfaction problem in the cross-border audit trail. The Axiom blog names it informally. The EDPB names it as a policy problem. Nobody has done the formal information-flow model showing precisely where the three regimes are satisfiable simultaneously and where they are provably not. **That formal model — a decision procedure showing under what conditions all three can hold — is genuinely novel and defensible.** The crypto-erasure mechanism then becomes the *answer* the model produces, not the contribution itself.

**Candidate 2 — The information-logistics formalism (most HiMolde-aligned, moderately novel).**
The structural analogy between cross-border data-retention conflict and physical cross-border logistics under conflicting jurisdictional record-keeping has not been formalised. The ICC brief treats data-as-supply-chain rhetorically. Nobody has built the actual mapping: audit log = customs documentation, retention floor = mandatory record-keeping, erasure right = certified destruction, and then applied *logistics optimisation methods* (which Tiger has from HiMolde — VRP, MIP, scenario planning) to the compliance-reconciliation problem. **This is where your degree becomes the contribution rather than a backdrop.**

**Candidate 3 — The Norwegian SPE-fragmentation finding (empirically grounded, narrow).**
The SPUHiN quote about OneDrive/disconnected-PCs is a genuine, citable, under-discussed empirical fact: Norwegian secondary-use processing is fragmented far below the NORTRE substrate. A contribution that designs *for* fragmentation rather than assuming homogeneity is defensible but narrow.

## My clinical recommendation

The thesis is currently aimed at Candidate-3-level novelty (apply known mechanism in Norwegian context). That is a pass, not an A.

**To reach genuine A-grade defensible novelty, the contribution should be reframed around Candidate 1 + Candidate 2 combined:**

> A formal constraint model of the audit-retention/erasure/deletion conflict in cross-border health data, expressed in information-logistics terms, with crypto-erasure-by-invalidation as the derived reconciliation mechanism, demonstrated on synthetic Norwegian data.

The crypto-erasure mechanism stops being the headline and becomes the *solution the formal analysis produces*. The novelty moves up a level — from "we applied X" to "we formally characterised a problem nobody had modelled, and derived a solution." That is the difference between a B+ and an A.

## What this requires before we can proceed

This is not a framing tweak. It needs new research to confirm the novelty holds:

1. **A targeted search** to confirm nobody has formally modelled the three-regime constraint (if someone has, Candidate 1 collapses and we fall back).
2. **A targeted search** on whether logistics/operations-research methods have been applied to data-compliance reconciliation (if yes, Candidate 2 weakens).
3. **A search** on formal models of GDPR-Art-17-vs-retention generally (legal informatics literature — there may be formal-methods work we have not surfaced).

If all three come back clear, we have genuine, defensible, A-grade novelty. If they do not, we know exactly where we stand and we calibrate the claim honestly.
